analysis:
Change: new ServiceDrain.relaunchDrainedProvider (ServiceDrain+Recovery.swift:46-53) wraps the stop and restart of a drained provider in `defer { rearm(explicitConfig) }`. UpdateCommand.restartInstalledProvider (UpdateCommand.swift:163-166) now calls it, so the watchdog is re-armed on failure as well as success. Previously rearmWatchdog ran only after a successful restart, leaving the provider down with no auto-recovery if the restart failed. The rearm logic is unchanged: explicit config wins, else the installed path; try? swallows errors; no new inputs, privileges or network surface. The new test file only exercises the hook with spies.

Security relevance is availability and recovery (T-043, T-047, T-057). This restores recovery on failure paths and is net positive.

Points for a deeper pass, not findings:
1. On failure, rearm now runs inside the do block before the catch calls session.release() and updater.cancelPendingCandidateAttempt (UpdateCommand.swift:167-170). The watchdog could act on pending candidate state (rollback or quarantine) concurrently with the cancel. I did not see watchdog or SelfUpdater lease and state-machine source, so this is unverified.
2. rearm also runs when stopDrainedProvider itself throws before the old process stopped. It is likely harmless, but the arm/disarm decision is not visible here.
3. Config fallback: if explicitConfig is nil, the watchdog uses its installed config path, as before.

No evidence of a regression against the threat model (T-043 watchdog authority is the same replaceable binary, unchanged). The relevant canonical text (T-041) is unrelated to this PR.
